title: The Healing at Bethesda and the Son Who Works Like the Father
summary: At a pool in Jerusalem Jesus heals a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years, telling him to pick up his mat and walk on the Sabbath. When the religious authorities object, Jesus answers that he is working as his Father works, and they seek to kill him for making himself equal with God. The rest of the chapter is Jesus' long defense: the Son gives life and judges with the Father's authority, and a line of witnesses, John the Baptist, Jesus' works, the Father, and the Scriptures with Moses, testifies to him.
story:
The first four chapters of John have been mostly welcome and wonder: the wine at Cana, Nicodemus by night, the Samaritan woman and her town, the official's son healed at a distance. Chapter 5 is a turning point. For the first time a sign provokes open hostility, and for the first time we read that the authorities were trying to kill Jesus (verse 18). From here the Gospel moves under a gathering shadow, and the question of Jesus' identity becomes a question of life and death for him as well as for his hearers. The chapter also sets the pattern for the chapters that follow: a sign, a controversy, and a discourse in which Jesus explains what the sign means about who he is. Chapter 6 will follow the same pattern in Galilee with the feeding of the five thousand, and chapter 7 will return to this healing, when Jesus asks why the authorities are angry that he made a whole man well on the Sabbath (7:21-23).

Much of what John will say about the Father and the Son is first laid out here. The Son does nothing on his own, yet whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise; the Father has given him life in himself and all judgment; the dead will hear his voice. The chapter ends not with a verdict on Jesus but with a verdict on his hearers, as the accused becomes the judge and Moses, in whom they hoped, becomes their accuser. It is the first of the great trial scenes that run through the Gospel until Jesus stands before Pilate.
historical:
Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for an unnamed feast of the Jews (verse 1). Interpreters have proposed nearly every festival. Irenaeus, around AD 180, took it as the second Passover of Jesus' ministry (Against Heresies 2.22.3); John Chrysostom thought it Pentecost (Homily 36 on John); others have argued for Tabernacles, Purim, or the New Year. Some manuscripts read ‘the feast’, which would point to a particular festival (see the text note), but the best witnesses read ‘a feast’, and John, who names Passover, Tabernacles, and Dedication elsewhere, leaves this one open. The chronology of Jesus' ministry does not depend on it.

The pool stood north of the temple near the Sheep Gate, the gate in the city wall rebuilt by the priests under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:1, 3:32, 12:39) and probably so named because sheep for sacrifice were brought in there. Manuscripts spell its name Bethesda, Bethzatha, or Bethsaida. Bethzatha resembles Bezetha, the name Josephus gives to the new quarter of the city north of the temple (Jewish War 5.151). The copper scroll from Qumran Cave 3, an inventory of hidden treasure written before AD 68, lists a hiding place at Beth Eshdatayin, ‘in the pool where you enter its small basin’ (3Q15 11:12-13); the name has a Hebrew dual ending, ‘the house of the two pools’, and many scholars take it as the pool John names, though the reading has been debated. Excavations on the property of the White Fathers at the Church of St. Anne, from the work of the architect Conrad Schick in the late nineteenth century to the 1960s, uncovered two large rock-cut reservoirs separated by a broad rock partition. Colonnades along the four sides and one across the dividing wall would give exactly the five covered colonnades of verse 2. For a long time some critics treated John's five porticoes as symbolic invention, perhaps for the five books of Moses; the discovery has made many more willing to credit the Gospel's knowledge of Jerusalem before its destruction in AD 70.

What the pools were used for in Jesus' day is debated. The northern pool was a reservoir; the southern pool, which had broad steps, may have served as a ritual immersion pool for pilgrims, as Shimon Gibson (Proche-Orient Chrétien 55, 2005) and Urban von Wahlde have argued. East of the pools, excavators found small basins, caves, and votive offerings from a Roman healing sanctuary dedicated to Asclepius, the Greek god of healing, and to Serapis, including a votive foot with a dedication and a Roman coin of Aelia Capitolina showing Serapis. That sanctuary belongs to the city Hadrian rebuilt as Aelia Capitolina after AD 135; whether a popular healing cult already gathered at the waters in Jesus' day is uncertain, though verse 7 shows that people believed the stirred water could heal. A Byzantine church was built over the site in the fifth century and a Crusader church later, and the Crusader Church of St. Anne still stands beside the ruins.

The man's thirty-eight years may recall Deuteronomy 2:14, where Israel's years of wandering from Kadesh-barnea until the Brook of Zered were thirty-eight, until the whole faithless generation had died; the echo is possible but uncertain, and John does not draw it out. The opponents are called simply the Jews. In John's Gospel the Greek word Ioudaioi can mean Jews in general, Judeans (people of Judea as distinct from Galileans), or, very often, the religious authorities in Jerusalem. Here it plainly means the last: the people who question the healed man, who can persecute Jesus, and who plan his death are the leaders around the temple, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his disciples, and the healed man are all Jews. The distinction matters because these passages were later used by Christians to blame the Jewish people collectively for the death of Jesus, a charge that fed centuries of contempt, expulsions, and violence and was exploited in modern antisemitic propaganda. The Roman Catholic Church formally rejected the charge of collective Jewish guilt in its 1965 declaration Nostra Aetate (section 4), and most churches now read John with this history in view.
cultural:
The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest commanded in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:8-11), was one of the chief marks of Jewish identity in the Roman world. The commandment forbade work but didn't define it, so teachers worked out what counted. The prophets had already singled out carrying: “do not carry a load or bring it through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day” (Jeremiah 17:21), and Nehemiah enforced the rule against traders (Nehemiah 13:15-19). The Mishnah, a collection of rabbinic rulings written down about AD 200 but preserving older tradition, lists thirty-nine main categories of forbidden work, ending with carrying an object from one domain to another (m. Shabbat 7:2). It also rules that one who carries a living person on a bed is not liable even for the bed, because the bed is secondary to the person, while one who carries an empty bed or a corpse on a bed is liable (m. Shabbat 10:5). Carrying a mat through the city by itself fell squarely under the prohibition, which is why the authorities object to the man before they ask about his healing (verse 10).

Healing itself raised a separate question. Later rabbinic law held that any doubt of danger to life overrides the Sabbath (m. Yoma 8:6), but a man ill for thirty-eight years was in no immediate danger, and a teacher who healed him on the Sabbath rather than the next day would seem to be making a point. He was. Jewish thinkers also recognized that God himself does not stop working on the Sabbath: he keeps the world in being, gives life, and judges. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher contemporary with Jesus, wrote that God never ceases from making, and that as it is the nature of fire to burn, so it is God's nature to create (Allegorical Interpretation 1.5-6). Jesus' reply in verse 17 builds on that shared conviction and applies it to himself. That is why his hearers understood him to be claiming equality with God. Philo, in the same work, calls the mind that thinks itself equal to God self-loving and godless (Allegorical Interpretation 1.49), and 2 Maccabees has the dying persecutor Antiochus IV confess that no mortal should think himself equal to God (2 Maccabees 9:12). To claim equality with God was, in Jewish ears, the very definition of arrogance and blasphemy, a charge the authorities make again in 10:33.

The discourse draws on the customs of family and law. A son in the ancient world learned his father's trade by watching him at work, and C. H. Dodd (More New Testament Studies, 1968) argued that verses 19 and 20 contain a small parable of the apprenticed son who does what he sees his father doing and whom the father loves and shows everything. The Mishnah states that a man's agent is like the man himself (m. Berakhot 5:5), so to dishonor the one sent is to dishonor the sender (verse 23). In court, the Law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and the Mishnah states the principle that a person cannot testify on his own behalf (m. Ketubbot 2:9); Jesus concedes the rule (verse 31) and then calls other witnesses. Study of the Law was held to bring life; Hillel is remembered as saying ‘the more Torah, the more life’ (m. Avot 2:7), and the book of Baruch says that all who hold fast to wisdom's law will live (Baruch 4:1). Jesus agrees that the Scriptures bear on eternal life, but says their testimony points to him (verse 39). Moses was remembered above all as Israel's intercessor, who pleaded for the people when God's anger burned (Exodus 32:11-14); Deuteronomy had also placed the Book of the Law beside the ark “as a witness against you” (Deuteronomy 31:26). Jesus turns the intercessor into the accuser. The lamp of verse 35 may recall God's promise, “I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one” (Psalm 132:17), and Sirach's praise of Elijah, whose word burned like a torch (Sirach 48:1), fitting for the one who came in the spirit of Elijah.
literary:
The chapter has two movements: a short healing story with its controversy (verses 1 to 18) and a long speech (verses 19 to 47). The healing is told with irony and restraint. The man never asks for healing, answers Jesus' question with a complaint, does not know Jesus' name, blames the man who healed him when challenged about the mat, and afterward reports Jesus to the authorities. He is the opposite of the man born blind in chapter 9, whose story runs in close parallel (a pool, a Sabbath healing, the healed man questioned by authorities, Jesus finding him afterward) but who grows in insight and confesses Jesus under pressure. John seems to intend the contrast.

The speech has two parts. Verses 19 to 30 set out the Son's relation to the Father, framed by an inclusio: “the Son can do nothing by Himself” (verse 19) and “I can do nothing by Myself” (verse 30). Three solemn ‘Truly, truly’ sayings (verses 19, 24, 25) mark its steps: the Son does what the Father does; whoever hears and believes has eternal life; the dead will hear the Son's voice and live. The section holds together two ways of speaking about the last things. In verses 24 and 25 the hour ‘has now come’ and believers have already crossed from death to life; in verses 28 and 29 the hour ‘is coming’ when all in the graves will come out to resurrection. Rudolf Bultmann assigned the future sayings to a later church editor, but most interpreters now read the tension as deliberate: eternal life begins now and is completed at the resurrection.

Verses 31 to 47 turn into something like a courtroom argument, part of what A. E. Harvey (Jesus on Trial, 1976) and Andrew Lincoln (Truth on Trial, 2000) have called the lawsuit motif that runs through the whole Gospel. Jesus concedes that his own word alone would not stand (verse 31) and calls his witnesses in turn: John the Baptist, the works the Father gave him, the Father himself, and the Scriptures, with Moses as the last witness, who becomes the prosecutor. The word martureō, ‘testify’, occurs seven times and its noun four times. By the end the roles are reversed: the accused speaks as judge, and his accusers stand charged with not having God's love in them and with seeking glory from one another. The chapter's place in the Gospel has also been discussed. Because chapter 4 ends in Galilee, chapter 5 is set in Jerusalem, and chapter 6 opens beside the Sea of Galilee, Bultmann proposed that chapters 5 and 6 had been transposed and that the original order was 4, 6, 5, 7; few now accept a rearrangement, and John's scenes move by theme as much as by itinerary.

outline.t: Jesus heals the invalid at the pool of Bethesda
The Sabbath controversy and the claim of equality with God
The Son gives life and judges with the Father's authority
The witnesses: John, the works, the Father, the Scriptures
Seeking glory from people, and Moses as accuser

doctrines.note: The Son “can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does” (verse 19). John holds together real distinction and full unity: the Son is sent and obedient, and he is also to be honored “just as they honor the Father” (verse 23). The Father has granted the Son to have life in himself (verse 26), language the church later read as the eternal generation of the Son. The church's confession of one God in three persons grew from passages like this.

Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath but claims the Father's own freedom within it: “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working” (verse 17). God's rest from creation never meant idleness in giving life and judging, and the Son shares that work. The Sabbath's rest is fulfilled, not cancelled, when the one who gives life restores a man on the day of rest.

The Father “has assigned all judgment to the Son” (verse 22), because he is the Son of Man of Daniel 7. Judgment is both present and future: whoever believes “has crossed over from death to life” and will not come under judgment (verse 24), and at the last all will come out of the graves to a resurrection of life or of judgment (verse 29).

“The hour is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out” (verses 28-29). The Son who gives life now to those who hear him will raise the dead bodily at the end, righteous and wicked alike, echoing Daniel 12:2. Spiritual life now and bodily resurrection later are two stages of one gift.

Jesus says the Scriptures are “the very words that testify about Me” (verse 39), and that Moses “wrote about Me” (verse 46). Diligent study of the Bible is not the same as hearing it; its purpose is to lead the reader to the one it points toward, and refusing him is refusing Moses.

words.note: Ergazomai, to work, be active, do. It occurs 40 times in the New Testament and eight times in John, and the related noun ergon, work, 27 times in John. In verse 17 Jesus uses the verb of both the Father and himself: the Father is at his work to this day, and so is he. The word ties the healing to God's ongoing work of sustaining and giving life, which even the Sabbath doesn't interrupt. John calls Jesus' deeds his works, given him by the Father to accomplish (verse 36), and they testify that the Father sent him.

Isos, equal, the same in size, quantity, or quality. It occurs only eight times in the New Testament, once in John (verse 18), and it appears in Philippians 2:6, where Christ did not consider equality with God something to be grasped. The narrator explains the authorities' fury: Jesus was “calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God”. The rest of the chapter does not deny the charge but explains it: the Son's equality is not a rival claim to independence, as the accusers suppose, but a perfect sharing in the Father's work and honor.

Hugiēs, healthy, sound, whole. It occurs 11 times in the New Testament, six times in John, five of them in this chapter (verses 6, 9, 11, 14, 15) and once in 7:23, where Jesus looks back on this day as the one on which he made a whole man well. Jesus' question in verse 6 is literally ‘Do you want to become whole?’, and the word recurs like a refrain through the controversy, keeping the healing itself before the reader while the authorities talk only about the mat.

Krisis, judgment. It occurs 47 times in the New Testament, 11 in John, and five in this chapter. It can mean the act of judging, a legal decision, or, in a negative sense, condemnation. In John it carries all of these: the Son has authority to judge (verses 22 and 27), the one who believes “will not come under judgment” (verse 24), meaning condemnation, and the evildoers rise to a resurrection of judgment (verse 29). The Son's judgment is just because he seeks the will of the one who sent him (verse 30).

Timaō, to honor, to show respect or reverence. It occurs 21 times in the New Testament and four times in verse 23 alone. The commandment to honor father and mother uses it in the Greek Old Testament (Exodus 20:12), and the prophets complain that people honor God with their lips (Isaiah 29:13). Here the claim is extraordinary: all should honor the Son just as they honor the Father, and whoever withholds honor from the Son withholds it from the Father. No Jewish teacher would say this of an agent, however exalted, unless the agent shared the sender's divine standing.

Zōē, life. It occurs 135 times in the New Testament, 36 times in John, and seven times in this chapter. In John it usually means eternal life, the life of the age to come given now to those who believe (verse 24). Verse 26 speaks of the Father having “life in Himself” and granting the Son to have life in himself, a phrase that the Old Testament implies of God alone, the living God who is the source of all life (Psalm 36:9, Jeremiah 2:13). The Son does not merely receive life as a creature does; he has it in himself and gives it to whom he wishes (verse 21).

Martureō, to testify, bear witness. It occurs 76 times in the New Testament and 33 times in John, more than in any other book, and seven times in this chapter, with the noun marturia four more times. BDAG gives its sense as confirming or attesting something on the basis of personal knowledge. Witness is one of John's central themes: the Baptist came to bear witness (1:7), the Gospel presents itself as testimony (19:35, 21:24), and here Jesus summons witnesses as in a trial, insisting that the testimony that matters is the Father's.

Graphē, a writing, Scripture. It occurs 50 times in the New Testament and 12 times in John, always of the sacred writings of Israel. Verse 39 uses the plural, the Scriptures, as a whole. The verb that goes with it, ereunaō, means to search or examine closely, and the form can be read either as a statement (‘You search the Scriptures’, most modern versions) or as a command (‘Search the scriptures’, KJV). The point either way is that the Scriptures are to be read for their witness to the one they point to, and that careful study can still miss him.

christ:
This chapter is one of the New Testament's fullest statements of who Jesus is in relation to God. He works as the Father works (verse 17). He gives life as the Father gives life (verse 21), a power the Old Testament reserves to God, who kills and makes alive (Deuteronomy 32:39). He has life in himself (verse 26), something said of God alone. He will raise the dead with his voice (verse 28). He receives the honor due to the Father (verse 23). And he is the Son of Man of Daniel 7, given authority to judge (verse 27). In Daniel “One like the Son of Man” comes with the clouds of heaven and is given “dominion, glory, and kingship” (Daniel 7:13-14); verse 27 is the only place in the Gospels where the phrase appears without the Greek article, ‘a son of man’, closely matching the wording of Daniel. The authority to judge belongs to him because he is both the one who shares God's prerogatives and the human one who stands with those he judges. Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the God of Israel, 2008) has argued that texts like this include Jesus within the unique identity of Israel's one God by giving him the functions, giving life and final judgment, that Jewish monotheism reserved for God alone.

Yet he is also the Son who does nothing by himself, who seeks not his own will but the will of the one who sent him (verse 30), and who does not accept glory from people (verse 41). John's portrait refuses to make Jesus either a second, rival god or a mere prophet. He is the obedient Son who is equal with the Father, and the church's later confession that he is true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one being with the Father (the Nicene Creed of 325 and 381), is an attempt to say both things at once without letting go of either.

The Scriptures, John the Baptist, the works, and the Father all testify to him, and Moses above all “wrote about Me” (verse 46), in the promise of a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:18), in the pattern of the exodus and the manna that chapter 6 will take up, and in the whole story the Law tells. The healing of a man who could not walk for thirty-eight years becomes a small picture of what the Son does: he speaks, and those who cannot help themselves get up. Isaiah had promised that in the day of God's coming “the lame will leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6); here the one through whom God comes tells a lame man to rise, and he walks.
interpretation:
Early readers were drawn first to the pool. Tertullian (On Baptism 5, around AD 200) read the angel who stirred the water as a figure of the angel present at baptism, and his use shows that the tradition later written into verse 4 was known by his day. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 2.22.3) used the feast of verse 1 to show that Jesus' ministry lasted more than one year. John Chrysostom preached on the chapter in Antioch beginning with Homily 36 on John, where he took the feast as Pentecost and praised the man's patience through thirty-eight years. Augustine (Tractate on John 17) read the five porticoes as the five books of Moses, which expose the sick but cannot heal them, and the thirty-eight years as forty, the number of the Law, lacking two, the two commandments of love.

The discourse became a battleground in the fourth-century debates about the Son. Arius and his followers pointed to verses 19, 26, and 30 (the Son can do nothing by himself; the Father granted him life; he seeks the will of the one who sent him) as proof that the Son was a creature subordinate to the Father. Athanasius (Discourses against the Arians, book 3), Hilary of Poitiers (On the Trinity, book 7), and Augustine (On the Trinity 2.1.3) answered that such sayings describe the Son's relation of origin from the Father, and his work in the form of a servant, not an inferiority of nature, and they pointed to verses 18, 21, and 23. That reading shaped the Nicene confession. In the Reformation, Calvin's commentary (1553) stressed the Son's authority to give life by his word, and the King James Version's imperative ‘Search the scriptures’ (verse 39) became a Protestant watchword for personal Bible reading.

Modern scholarship has asked about sources, order, and history. Bultmann (1941) proposed that chapters 5 and 6 had been transposed and assigned the future resurrection of verses 28 and 29 to a church editor. C. H. Dodd (1968) found an older parable of the apprenticed son in verses 19 and 20. The excavation of the double pool at St. Anne's changed the discussion of John's historical reliability about Jerusalem. J. Louis Martyn (History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel, 1968) argued that the Gospel's conflicts with ‘the Jews’ reflect a later struggle between the Johannine believers and synagogue authorities, a thesis still debated, and Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz (Cast Out of the Covenant, 2018) have pressed Christian readers to face how the chapter's language has been heard. The Pontifical Biblical Commission's study The Jewish People and Their Sacred Scriptures in the Christian Bible (2001) addressed John's usage directly.

In liturgy, the Revised Common Lectionary offers verses 1 to 9 as an alternative Gospel on the sixth Sunday of Easter in Year C, and the Orthodox Church keeps the fourth Sunday of Pascha (counting Easter Day as the first) as the Sunday of the Paralytic. In art, Tintoretto painted the pool for the church of San Rocco in Venice (1559); Bartolomé Esteban Murillo's Christ Healing the Paralytic at the Pool of Bethesda (1667-1670), painted for the Hospital de la Caridad in Seville, hangs in the National Gallery in London; and William Hogarth painted The Pool of Bethesda (1736) without fee for the great staircase of St Bartholomew's Hospital in London, with sufferers thought to be modeled on the hospital's own patients. The name Bethesda was given to hospitals, chapels, and charities across the English-speaking world, a sign of how the story came to stand for Christ's care for the sick.
text:
Verses 3b and 4 are the chapter's best-known textual question. Later manuscripts add at the end of verse 3 that the sick were ‘waiting for the moving of the water’, and then verse 4: that an angel went down at certain seasons into the pool and stirred the water, and whoever stepped in first after the stirring was healed of whatever disease he had. The earliest and best witnesses, including P66, P75, Codex Sinaiticus, and Codex Vaticanus, lack both, and other manuscripts that include them mark them as doubtful or word them differently. Most scholars think the words were added as an explanatory note drawn from a popular belief that verse 7 reflects, and modern versions omit verse 4 or put it in a footnote; the BSB omits it and keeps the verse number. The King James Version and the New King James Version include it.

Other variants are smaller. In verse 1 most early manuscripts, including P66, P75, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and Bezae, read ‘a feast’, while Sinaiticus, Ephraemi, and others read ‘the feast’, which would point to one particular festival. In verse 2 the pool is Bethesda in Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, and most later manuscripts, Bethzatha in Sinaiticus, and Bethsaida in P75 and Vaticanus; the Greek also leaves unstated what the sheep place was, so the KJV has ‘by the sheep market’ and most modern versions ‘near the Sheep Gate’. In verse 16 later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add that the Jews ‘sought to slay him’, anticipating verse 18.

Translation choices also differ. In verse 27 the phrase has no article, huios anthrōpou, which some render ‘because He is the Son of Man’ (BSB, ESV) and others ‘because he is the son of man’ or ‘a son of man’, stressing his humanity. In verse 39 the verb ereunate can be indicative or imperative: the KJV has ‘Search the scriptures’, while modern versions read ‘You search’ or ‘You pore over’ the Scriptures, which fits the rebuke that follows.

teach.big: Jesus, the Son who works as the Father works, has the Father's own authority to give life and to judge, and every witness, the Baptist, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures, calls us to come to him and live.

outline.t: Jesus seeks out a man who has given up hope and has no one to help him, and his word does what years of waiting could not.
Religious rules can blind people to grace: the authorities see a mat carried on the Sabbath and miss a man restored, and the healed man is warned that the worse danger is sin.
Jesus claims to share the Father's unceasing work, and his hearers rightly understand that he is making himself equal with God.
The Son's equality with the Father is not rivalry but perfect sharing: he does what the Father does, gives life, judges, and is to be honored as the Father is.
Eternal life begins now for whoever hears and believes, and it will be completed when the Son's voice raises the dead; the judge of all is the obedient Son of Man.
God has not left us without witnesses: the Baptist, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures all point to Jesus, but study without coming to him leaves us without life.
The deepest obstacle to faith is the love of human approval; those who seek glory from one another cannot believe, and Moses himself will accuse those who refuse the one he wrote about.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first builds a psychology sermon on verse 6, as if Jesus were diagnosing the man's secret wish to stay ill. The question may probe, but the man's answer is a lament that no one helps him, and Jesus heals him without requiring any right answer or even faith; the story is about Jesus' initiative. The second takes verse 14 (‘Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you’) as proof that illness is always punishment for sin. John himself rules that out in 9:3; verse 14 warns this man that sin has worse consequences than paralysis, without explaining his illness. The third treats the Sabbath controversy as Jesus against Judaism or against rest. Jesus argues from Jewish convictions about God's work and fulfills the Sabbath rather than discarding it.

Teachers should also avoid setting Jesus against the Bible on the basis of verse 39, as if the Scriptures could be bypassed for direct experience of him; he says they testify about him, and he appeals to Moses as a witness. Avoid reading verse 29 (‘those who have done good’) as teaching salvation by works apart from faith; in John the work God requires is to believe in the one he sent (6:29), and good deeds show that a person has come to the light (3:21). Avoid softening verses 19 and 30 into a Jesus who is less than God, or verses 18 and 23 into a Jesus who is a second, independent deity. And avoid preaching ‘the Jews’ of this chapter as a picture of Jewish people; they are particular authorities in Jerusalem, and the church's history with these verses requires care.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses hard on people living with chronic illness or disability, and on those who love them. Thirty-eight years of waiting, and a man who says, “I have no one to help me”, will describe some people in the room exactly. Honor that; do not suggest that they remain ill because they lack desire or faith, and do not use verse 14 to hint that their suffering is punishment, which John 9:3 forbids. Many in the room have prayed for healing that has not come. The story shows Jesus choosing one man out of a great number of sick people, which is itself a hard truth, and it is honest to say that most were not healed that day; the healing is a sign of the life the Son will give fully at the resurrection (verses 28-29). The chapter also speaks to those who are lonely and without advocates, and to people wounded by religious communities that cared more about rules than about them. Finally, because these verses have been used against Jewish people, teach them in a way no Jewish neighbor would have reason to fear.

hard.q: Does John's language about ‘the Jews’ make the Gospel anti-Jewish?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real, and its sharpest statements come from Jewish scholars and from Christian historians who have studied its effects. John uses Ioudaioi about seventy times, often for those who oppose Jesus, and in this chapter they persecute him and seek to kill him (verses 16 and 18); later in the Gospel Jesus tells some of them that they are of their father the devil (8:44). Rosemary Radford Ruether (Faith and Fratricide, 1974) argued that hostility to Judaism was built into early Christian claims about Christ, and Adele Reinhartz (Cast Out of the Covenant, 2018) has argued that John's rhetoric is designed to separate its readers from Jewishness and cannot simply be explained away as referring to a few leaders. Historians have documented how these passages were read aloud in Holy Week and used to justify contempt, expulsion, and violence against Jewish communities for centuries.

Christian interpreters have responded in several ways. Many note that the term often means the Judean religious leadership, not the people as a whole, that it can also mean Judeans as distinct from Galileans, and that John also uses it neutrally or positively: Jesus says that “salvation is from the Jews” (4:22), and many Jews believe in him in chapters 11 and 12. J. Louis Martyn (History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel, 1968) argued that the Gospel's sharp tone reflects a painful later conflict between Jewish believers in Jesus and synagogue authorities, so that it records a quarrel within a Jewish family rather than a verdict on a people, though his reconstruction has been contested. The Roman Catholic Church, in Nostra Aetate (1965), rejected the charge that Jews then or now are collectively guilty of Christ's death, and the Pontifical Biblical Commission (2001) urged that John's language be read in its historical setting. Others hold that no single explanation removes the difficulty and that the church must read these texts with repentance for how they have been used.

What the text itself shows is that every main character in this chapter is Jewish, including Jesus, and that the opposition comes from a particular leadership in a particular place and time. Jesus appeals to Moses and the Scriptures as God's witnesses, not as a rival faith. To turn the chapter into a charge against a people is a misreading, and one with a long and grievous history.

hard.q: If the Son can do nothing by himself and receives life from the Father, is he really equal with God?
hard.a:
The objection is ancient and serious. Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria in the early fourth century, and his followers pointed to verses 19, 26, 27, and 30: the Son can do nothing by himself, the Father has granted him to have life in himself, the Father has given him authority, and he seeks not his own will but the will of the one who sent him. On their reading these words show that the Son is a glorious creature, the first and highest of God's works, but not God in the same sense as the Father. Unitarian Christians since the Reformation and Jehovah's Witnesses today read the chapter similarly, and some historians of doctrine have argued that the later creeds say more than John does.

The church's answer, given by Athanasius (Discourses against the Arians, book 3), Hilary of Poitiers (On the Trinity, book 7), and Augustine (On the Trinity 2.1.3), is that the same passage attributes to the Son what belongs to God alone: he does whatever the Father does (verse 19), gives life to whom he wishes (verse 21), is the judge of all (verse 22), is to be honored just as the Father is (verse 23), and has life in himself (verse 26). A creature cannot have life in himself, and no creature may receive the honor due to God (Isaiah 42:8). The sayings about dependence describe the Son's eternal relation to the Father, from whom he is begotten, and his obedience in the incarnation, not an inferiority of nature; the evangelist himself reports without correction that Jesus was making himself equal with God (verse 18). The Nicene Creed (325, expanded 381) confesses the Son as true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one being with the Father, and this is the church's first-order confession. Among modern scholars Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the God of Israel, 2008) has argued that John includes Jesus within the unique identity of the one God of Israel.

Within that confession Christians still debate a second-order question: whether the Son's obedience to the Father belongs only to his mission in the flesh, or also expresses an eternal order of relation within the Trinity. In 2016 Wayne Grudem and Bruce Ware, who hold that the Son eternally submits to the Father in role though not in nature, debated Kevin Giles and Millard Erickson, who reject that view, at the Evangelical Theological Society, and theologians such as Carl Trueman and Liam Goligher argued that talk of eternal submission departs from Nicene teaching. Readers should know that the confession of the Son's full deity is not in dispute among these writers; the debate concerns how to describe the Father-Son relation that John 5 portrays.

observe: What question does Jesus ask the man at the pool, and how does the man answer it?
What reason does the narrator give in verse 18 for the authorities' determination to kill Jesus?
What four witnesses does Jesus call in verses 31 to 47?
interpret: How does Jesus' saying ‘My Father is at His work, and I too am working’ answer the charge of breaking the Sabbath, and why did his hearers take it as a claim to equality with God?
How can the Son both ‘do nothing by Himself’ and do ‘whatever the Father does’? What does this say about the relation of Father and Son?
What does Jesus mean when he says that eternal life is already possessed now (verse 24) and that the dead will come out of their graves at the coming hour (verses 28-29)?
apply: The man said he had no one to help him. Who around you is without help, and what would it mean for you to go to them?
Where has your reading of Scripture become an end in itself rather than a way of coming to Jesus?
Jesus says the love of praise from others keeps people from believing. Whose approval do you seek most, and how does it shape what you are willing to believe or do?
